summary: DS-Lite reserved a small IPv4 block for a particular tunnel element. This document generalizes that reservation so it can also be used when an IPv6 transition solution needs to number a non-routed IPv4 interface.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo generalizes the IPv4 prefix 192.0.0.0/29 for IPv6 transition solutions that need an IPv4 address on a non-routed interface. It says a host must not run overlapping continuity solutions at the same time.

questions: what is the ipv4 service continuity prefix
how does 464xlat get an ipv4 address
subtitle: A shared IPv4 prefix for non-routed interfaces used by IPv6 transition solutions.

tldr.problem: DS-Lite had a reserved IPv4 prefix, and other IPv6 transition systems also needed a non-routed IPv4 address range.
tldr.mechanism: The memo generalizes the reservation of 192.0.0.0/29 as the IPv4 Service Continuity Prefix for transition solutions that do not send packets from it onto the wire.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7335 updates RFC 6333 and prohibits simultaneous active solutions that create overlapping use of the prefix on a node.

today: RFC 7335 is a Proposed Standard and updates RFC 6333. The unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 7335.

sections.title: A Prefix for IPv4 Service Continuity
sections.content:
RFC 6333 reserved 192.0.0.0/29 for the Basic Bridging BroadBand (B4) element in Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite). RFC 7335 generalizes that reservation to other cases where an IPv6 transition solution needs a number for a non-routed IPv4 interface.

The prefix may be used for IPv4 compatibility in an IPv6-only network when the system does not emit IPv4 packets from that prefix onto the wire. The generalization does not change its use in DS-Lite.
sections.plainLanguage: The prefix was reserved for DS-Lite and is now available to other IPv6 transition solutions with the same kind of non-routed IPv4 need. It is not used to send IPv4 packets onto the network.

sections.title: Use by 464XLAT and Other Solutions
sections.content:
464XLAT can place a customer-side translator (CLAT) in a host. The host needs an IPv4 address for its network stack and for applications to bind IPv4 sockets, even when the access network is IPv6-only. The address must be locally unique to avoid conflicts with other networks that may communicate with the CLAT.

The memo generalizes the DS-Lite prefix for 464XLAT and similar transition solutions rather than reserving a separate prefix for each one. A host MUST NOT enable two active IPv4 continuity solutions simultaneously in a way that gives a node overlapping 192.0.0.0/29 address space.
sections.plainLanguage: A host may need an IPv4 address for local applications even on an IPv6-only network. It must not run two active solutions that assign overlapping addresses from this prefix.

sections.title: IANA Registry and Security
sections.content: IANA changed the IPv4 Special-Purpose Address Registry name for 192.0.0.0/29 from DS-Lite to IPv4 Service Continuity Prefix. The memo says there are no new security considerations beyond those described in RFC 6333 and RFC 6877.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA updated the registry name to reflect the prefix's broader role. The memo adds no security considerations beyond those in the referenced specifications.

references.text: Durand, A., Droms, R., Woodyatt, J., and Y. Lee, "Dual-Stack Lite Broadband Deployments Following IPv4 Exhaustion", RFC 6333, August 2011.
Mawatari, M., Kawashima, M., and C. Byrne, "464XLAT: Combination of Stateful and Stateless Translation", RFC 6877, April 2013.
